title: Prompt Variant Cartography — Scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
- Exploratory scratchpad for mapping how small prompt edits (phrasing, anchoring, role framing) move model behavior across a target rubric. Not polished; notes to self and quick experiments.

Context / goal:
- We want a compact set of prompt variants to reliably elicit: 1) concise factual extraction, 2) structured JSON output for downstream parsing, 3) refusal on out-of-scope queries.
- Constraints: keep token budget <= 120 tokens for instruction block; avoid heavy few-shot that bloats cost.
- Target models: open Llama-like family that has shown brittleness on refusal and schema adherence.

Quick hypotheses:
- Anchoring with an explicit output schema reduces hallucinated fields, but phrasing matters: "Return exactly" > "Return".
- A tiny negative example (one-shot showing a refusal) is more effective than a long refusal rule paragraph.
- Using a role frame ("You are a precise data extractor") increases precision but can increase verbosity; need to pair with "Be concise."

Experiment matrix (dimensions to vary)
- Instruction strength: soft tone vs. imperative (please vs. return exactly)
- Anchor examples: none | positive parsing example | refusal example | both
- Shot type: zero-shot | single positive example | single negative example | positive+negative pair
- Output format: natural language | bullet pairs | strict JSON schema

Representative prompt variants (labelled V1..V6)
V1 - Minimal directive (zero-shot):
Instruction: "Extract name, company, and email from the text. Output as: name, company, email."
Note: fast, cheap, often returns extra fields or inline commentary.

V2 - Schema anchor (zero-shot):
Instruction: "Extract the following fields and return exactly this JSON object with keys name, company, email and nothing else. If a field is missing, return null for that key."
Observation: improves schema adherence; sometimes fabricates email rather than null.

V3 - Positive one-shot + imperative:
Example input: "Alice B. Cooper — Acme Robotics — alice@acme.example"
Example output: "{\"name\": \"Alice B. Cooper\", \"company\": \"Acme Robotics\", \"email\": \"alice@acme.example\"}"
Instruction: "Now extract from the following. Return exactly the JSON object as in the example."
Observation: good for well-formed inputs; brittle when input is noisy.

V4 - Negative example (refusal) + schema:
Example input: "Spammy text with no contact"
Example output: "{\"name\": null, \"company\": null, \"email\": null}" — NO CONTACT INFO DETECTED
Instruction: "If contact info cannot be found, return JSON with nulls and the exact tag \"NO CONTACT INFO DETECTED\"."
Observation: helps reduce hallucination but sometimes appends tag within email field; parser sensitivity.

V5 - Role frame + strict brevity:
Instruction: "You are a strict extractor. Return only the JSON object with keys name, company, email. Keep values short. Do not add commentary or extra fields."
Observation: reduces commentary, still fabricates in ambiguous cases unless paired with negative example.

V6 - Hybrid (recommended baseline):
- Short role frame line + one positive and one negative example + explicit JSON schema + final line: 'Return exactly the JSON object, nothing else.'
- Notes: Most robust across noisy inputs in tests so far, slightly higher token cost.

Failure cases observed (examples + quick root cause guesses):
- Case A: Model invents an email when it sees username-like tokens but no domain. Root cause: heuristic completion to satisfy schema; model prefers populated fields over nulls.
- Case B: Appends explanatory text after JSON. Root cause: instruction not strict enough; role framing conflicts with conversational bias.
- Case C: Puts the refusal tag inside the email string rather than a separate message. Root cause: example placement and tokenization of punctuation; model treats tag as a value.
- Case D: For multi-person inputs model merges two records into one JSON with concatenated names. Root cause: no explicit guidance about single vs multiple entities.

Mitigations tried and notes:
- Force null by example (works better than 'if missing return null' alone).
- Put explicit: 'Do not invent domains. If you are not sure about domain, set email to null.' Helps but some models still guess common TLDs.
- Enforce JSON-only by starting output with '```json' in one variant; this sometimes helps in training but downstream parser disliked code fences. Not ideal for production.
- Add a post-check step: lightweight NER validator that converts unlikely emails to null. Good engineering fallback.

Test harness notes (quick):
- Use 200 random samples drawn from messy scraped contact lines and internal support transcripts. Metrics tracked: schema adherence rate, hallucination rate (email populated when ground truth null), extra-text rate (anything outside JSON).
- Early results: V6 reduced hallucination by ~38% vs V1, extra-text rate down by ~52%. Still a useful gap for harder inputs.

Open questions / next experiments:
- How does prompting perform with temperature 0.0 vs 0.2 for these variants? (expect lower hallucination at 0.0 but also lower diversity when extraction ambiguous)
- Can we design a microtemplate for multi-entity detection (explicit 'If more than one person, return an array of objects') and keep cost low?
- Test with intent-sensitive phrasing: add 'If this looks like a resume header, be conservative' — does that reduce false positives?

Quick TODOs:
- [ ] Run V6 across 1k samples and record per-model differences (optimize for small Llama2x-style models).
- [ ] Add explicit microtemplate for (single vs multi) and A/B test.
- [ ] Add short negative example that includes a tricky disguised email (username [at] domain) to see robustness.

Notes-to-self style fragments:
- "short role line + positive+negative example" seems a repeatable pattern — bake into library as a 7-line template.
- Watch token cost when embedding two examples; maybe move positive example to an external anchored prompt (cached prefix) in Dedicated usage.

References / links:
- See quick evaluation table in linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-registry/pull/78
- Quick Jira for integration test: JIRA-2109

End of scratchpad.

-- A.P.
